problem: Existing human-aware navigation planners are each designed for a single context (crowd, or a specific indoor setting such as homes, offices or warehouses), so a different planner is needed for each new human-robot context. Multi-context planners are rare, and the one prior example was shown only with static humans.
motivation: Robots deployed in human environments meet very different situations: reactive crowd navigation and intricate indoor encounters such as narrow corridors or doors. Swapping algorithms per context is impractical. The paper proposes one tunable planner whose planning mode changes with the assessed situation.
key_idea: Extend the HATEB (Human-Aware Timed Elastic Band) local planner with multiple control-level planning modes, including a new Backoff-recovery mode, plus human-aware costmap layers and constraints, so one parameter-tunable system handles both crowd and intricate indoor contexts.
insight: Switching modes at the control level (SingleBand, DualBand, VelObs, Backoff-recovery) lets the planner solve situations a single mode cannot. The clearest case is the narrow corridor, where the baseline TPF/Lattice planner failed and HATEB succeeded through Backoff-recovery. The comparison also shows a trade-off: HATEB takes longer paths (for example 9.23 m vs 8.79 m in Open Space) but finishes faster (16.0 s vs 24.8 s) and keeps larger human distances when space allows. There is no ablation of individual components.
method: Human Safety and Human Visibility costmap layers: a 2D Gaussian around static humans and a half-Gaussian behind them, with a 3 m cutoff, added to the global and local costmaps via the human_layers ROS plugin.
Human path prediction: four services (PredictBehind, PredictGoal via Bayesian goal inference, PredictVelObs with 5 s velocity extrapolation, PredictExternal) supply human global paths.

HATEB local planner modes: SingleBand (robot band only), DualBand (bands for the 2 nearest dynamic humans), VelObs (bands only for moving humans, for crowds and entanglement) and Backoff-recovery, with situation-assessment-based transitions.

Backoff-recovery mode: triggered in VelObs mode when a human is within 2.5 m and the robot has been stuck for more than 10 s. The robot backs off slowly without turning its back, clears the way, waits for the human, then resumes, and can accept new goals while waiting.

New constraints: a Visibility constraint (half-Gaussian cost to avoid emerging suddenly from behind a human) and a Relative Velocity constraint (cost from relative velocity and distance, which slows the robot near humans). Both replace the TTC and TTCplus constraints.
Field-of-view and planning radius: ray tracing on the map restricts planning to visible humans within a 10 m radius, and human planning is limited to the 2 nearest humans to keep control real-time.

setting.backbone: HATEB (Timed Elastic Band optimization-based local planner) on the ROS navigation stack; no learned model
setting.observation: external human tracking (positions and velocities; OptiTrack mocap at 10 Hz on the real robot) plus a map with ray-traced field of view; robot laser costmaps
setting.action_space: continuous velocity commands (cmd_vel) to the base controller
setting.privileged: external human tracking and positions (simulator ground truth or OptiTrack mocap); known map

numbers_note: Not an embodied-navigation benchmark paper. The only quantitative table is a comparison with TPF on custom scenarios (see results); it is not a canonical benchmark.
results: On four custom simulated scenarios (mean of 10 runs), HATEB has a shorter total time than TPF in all three where both succeed (Open Space 16.01 s vs 24.77 s; Narrow Passage 17.80 s vs 27.16 s; Pillar Corridor 31.46 s vs 52.94 s). It also has a larger minimum human-robot distance in Open Space (1.29 m vs 0.95 m) and Pillar Corridor (0.89 m vs 0.76 m). TPF gives shorter paths and a better minimum distance in Narrow Passage (0.935 m vs 0.706 m), and it fails in Narrow Corridor, where HATEB completes the task (23.54 m, 48.39 s, 0.66 m). The system also navigates PedSim crowds and runs on a Pepper robot in open-space and corridor tests.
limitations: The per-loop optimization is computationally costly, and the control rate drops to 8-9 Hz in DualBand and VelObs modes.
Planning covers only the 2 nearest humans, and groups of people are not handled specially.
Evaluation is qualitative and small-scale: one baseline (TPF), 10 runs in four scenarios, and human tracking supplied externally. Real-robot results are only qualitative.
compares_to: Timed Path Follower (TPF) with Lattice Planner (Kollmitz et al.)
